❯ Without tools, explain in about 250 words how a lighthouse works: a heading, a list of its three main parts, and two    paragraphs.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
● How a Lighthouse Works                                                                                                                                                                                                                        
  A lighthouse is a tower that marks a dangerous or important point on the coast so that ships can navigate safely,     
  especially at night or in poor visibility. Its three main parts are:                                                  
                                                                                                                          - The light source. A lamp, once an oil or gas flame and now usually an LED, produces the beam.                       
  - The optic. A system of lenses and prisms, often a Fresnel lens, gathers the light from the lamp and focuses it into 
    a concentrated beam instead of letting it spread in all directions.                                                 
  - The rotating mechanism. A clockwork or motor turns the optic so the beam sweeps across the horizon. Each lighthouse 
    has its own flash pattern, so sailors can tell which light they are seeing.                                         
                                                                                                                        
  The lamp sits at the center of the optic, and the optic is mounted on a turntable or inside a rotating drum. Its      
  curved glass panels bend light that would otherwise escape upward or downward into a narrow horizontal band. The      
  result is a beam that is much brighter at sea than the bare flame would be, and the rotation makes it appear as a     
  flash rather than a steady glow.                                                                                      
                                                                                                                        
  The tower's height matters as well. A higher light can be seen from farther away, because the curve of the Earth      
  limits how far a light near the water can reach the horizon. Modern lighthouses often run automatically on solar or   
  mains power, and many now use GPS and radio beacons alongside the light, but the basic principle of a focused,        
  rotating beam that identifies a location has not changed for about two centuries.
